speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to comment on the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice. I do so because this is not the first time this point of order has been raised, and because I think it is a very serious and very important one.
In the last two or three days it has been contended by the Secretary of State and by the Minister of Justice that it is out of order for us to ask questions that conceivably we could ask when we get to the discussion of the budget resolutions, because the budget resolutions are set down as an order of the day. The two ministers mentioned have made reference to the fact that it is supposedly a rule of this house that we cannot on orders of the day ask questions that anticipate an order of the day. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a very important point and that it should be cleared up.
Obviously, if this dictum were to prevail, that hon. members could not ask questions that anticipate something that is set down as an order of the day somewhere on the order paper, we could soon get into the situation where we could not ask a single question, because once we get the estimates, legislation and the budget on the order paper everything is there and we would be blocked from asking anything.
I recognize that the reason the Secretary of State, the Minister of Justice and others try to make this point is that there is a phrase in Beauchesne's citation 171 (v) which reads, if I may put the prefix with it:
A question oral or written must not:
(v) anticipate an Order of the Day or other matters.
We are governed in this house by the rules, by the standing orders, that we have made.
[Mr. Diefenhaker J

Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms is not a rule book. It is a guide book containing many instances of things out of the past, a compilation of decisions and announcements which have been made. When we find an item such as this-
A question oral or written must not anticipate an Order of the Day or other matters.
-we should look to see where Dr. Beau-chesne got it. He helps us, because right after it, on page 148 of the fourth edition, there is in parenthesis a notation, M. 242. This refers us, if we take the trouble to look it up, to page 242 of Erskine May's thirteenth edition. If we look at that page we find that Dr. Beauchesne has reduced a sentence to a phrase, and I submit that in doing so he has done violence to the original sentence in May. May said discussion in anticipation upon an order of the day-and by the way, in May "order of the day" is in small letters while in Beauchesne it is capitalized, which makes quite a difference-by way of a question is not permitted.
This is the point I wish to make. There is a great deal of difference between being told we cannot ask a question that relates to something which is on the order paper, which is what Beauchesne seems to say and what the Secretary of State seems to say, and being told by May that we cannot, on the orders of the day, develop a discussion or a debate on something which is set down as an order for the day.
If one is to understand what is behind all this, he must go further. On page 242 of May's thirteenth edition, where appears the sentence I have just quoted-
Discussion in anticipation upon an order of the day or other matter by means of a question is not permitted.
-is a small figure 8 referring to a footnote at the bottom of the page. The next thing to do is to find out what is in that footnote. Well, it refers one to a couple of volumes of the Hansard of the United Kingdom House of Commons. There are, in fact, three incidents which come to light on following up the footnote in Beauchesne. Two of them happened in 1876 and one in 1896 in the House of Commons at Westminster.
I have read those Hansards to see what those incidents were. In each case a member of the House of Commons at Westminster, according to the rules and forms they have there, had filed a motion for a debate to take place later that day-the debate they have, for example, on the adjournment. Let me repeat; in each of these three cases a member of the United Kingdom House of Commons had filed a motion for a debate to take place later that day, and in each of these cases the very member who had filed such a notice

tried to anticipate the debate he was going to get, in a couple of cases on the adjournment, by asking a question.
One of the cases before the house at Westminster was a motion to set aside the adjournment rule to make such a debate possible. The Speaker pointed out that the motion was to be decided without amendment or debate. Once it had been decided the hon. member would get his debate, so he should not get a debate in anticipation. These are three specific cases, in each of which the Speaker of the House of Commons said "You"-the hon. member trying to do this today-"have no right to do this now because you are anticipating something you are going to get later in the day".
The Speaker in the British House of Commons did not lay down a general rule that for all time there were to be no questions on orders of the day which would anticipate matters on the order paper. There is no such rule in the British house, just as there is no such rule here.
In my view the Speaker of the British House of Commons was perfectly correct in admonishing the members concerned, twice in 1876 and once in 1896; but having regard to what May said on page 242, compressed by Beauchesne into the words which appear in citation 171(v) of his fourth edition, for the Secretary of State and the Minister of Justice to argue that because something is on the order paper-we may not discuss the budget resolutions until fall-we have no right to ask questions about it on orders of the day seems to me quite wrong.

We will not get the chance to debate the matter for a long time, and the assertion of the government that there is a rule which says we cannot do this is contrary to the traditions and practices both of the House of Commons at Westminster and our House of Commons in Canada.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF APPLICATION OF SALES TAX TO BUILDING MATERIALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there seems to be two points that have arisen in connection with the point of order. The first has to do with the urgency of questions, as submitted to the house by the Leader of the Opposition. On that point I should like to say what has been said more than once in the house, namely that if the questions are urgent surely there has been an opportunity to deal with that urgency over the last week or ten days, when all sorts of questions have arisen and have been asked of the government and more particularly of the Minister of Finance and answered by him.
With respect to the point raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre I should like to say to him, with respect, that he has overstated his case. I say that because the rule, as you have pointed out repeatedly, Mr. Speaker, laid down in citation 171 (v) is quite clear, namely that a question oral or written must not anticipate an order of the day or other matters. It is true that my hon. friend has attempted by referring to May, page 242, to explain at great length that that was not the meaning of the citation as outlined in 171 (v) of Beauchesne. However, if one looks a little further in Beauchesne one will find that in citation 173 (1) the answer is to be found to the argument made by the hon. member, and I should like to put it on the record. Citation 173 (1) of Beauchesne reads as follows:
On the Orders of the Day being called, members may ask members of the government to explain certain matters in accordance with practice, but it it not done under the authority of a standing order and therefore such questions may be either permitted or disallowed by the Speaker who must judge each case on its merits. The practice has been so long and so regularly in the house that, if not impossible, in my opinion, it would be inadvisable to stop it.
It seems to me, sir, that this is the answer to the question which has been raised, and it seems to me also that this is the ruling which was made on a previous occasion. Under the circumstances it would strike me that the questions, even though they would appear to hon. members to be urgent because of circumstances which change from day to day, cannot be anticipated until such time as the resolutions are before the house. I submit with respect, sir, that this is the manner in which this question should be disposed of.

I pursued the same course of inquiry and followed the references right back to 1876, and the case as stated by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre represents the situation as set out in the reference books. I think he is perfectly correct in drawing attention to the fact that Beauchesne in citation 171(v) has incorrectly capitalized the words "Order of the Day" and has thereby caused a misunderstanding of this particular problem. I also agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre that the Minister of Justice and Secretary of State have attempted to read into that citation in Beauchesne something which is not there. As a matter of fact, on page 1628 of Hansard the Secretary of State is recorded as saying this:
I think it is a rule of the house that questions are not to be put on the orders of the day about matters which are set down on the order paper for the consideration of the house.
As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre very properly pointed out, the order paper could embrace all subjects that conceivably could be brought before the House of Commons. Then, if this were accepted as the rule, we would be prohibited from asking questions on those subjects. We would be accused then of anticipating a debate which might be postponed for six months.
In order to complete the record I might indicate that the reference in Beauchesne to May's thirteenth edition can be found in May's sixteenth edition on page 359, and the subnote on that page is the same as the one in the thirteenth edition.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I consider that this is a very important matter which must be decided by your ruling, after you have had a chance to give careful consideration to it. May I point out that the other day when the Leader of the Opposition raised a point of order you dismissed it on the basis that he was relying on a rather ancient precedent which had been established in the House of Commons. I recall my own experience in June, 1956, when I raised a point of order and the Speaker dismissed it because he said it was archaic since it dated back to 1885. The one upon which Your Honour is relying, if you accept Beauchesne, dates back to 1876. As the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre points out, it has not been a rule of this house.

The house resumed, from Thursday, June 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Chevrier for the second reading of Bill No. C-74, respecting the department of industry.

When the house adjourned last night I was suggesting that this bill was inoperative because of the bifocal approach which has been made to this subject of industry. I had also pointed out that, as is well known to all members of the house, the Department of Trade and Commerce is one of the original departments of government going back to a time just after confederation. It is one of the senior departments of government, and one which I am sure all members will agree has been very efficiently administered and well run. Even when our opponents became very critical of the administration of the government of which I was a member they always excepted the Department of Trade and Commerce and admitted that it was an efficient department.
Well handled.

Well handled, yes. I think there was a feeling at one point that the Department of Trade and Commerce was more interested in trade than in other matters, more interested in buying and selling than in industry itself. I know that at one time representations were made by the manufacturers of this country on the subject. I think there was once a formal request in a brief of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association that there should be a department of industry. That was several years ago and, as I recall it, that representation has not been renewed latterly.

Establishment of Industry Department
It would appear to me, or at least it appeared to me some time ago, that there was real merit in the suggestion that perhaps the name of the department should be changed so that instead of "Trade and Commerce" it would be "Industry and Commerce" so as to recognize the important part industry plays in the development of this country. But that is a far cry from creating a new department entirely. Although it is true the emphasis in the department was originally on trade and commerce, latterly the department has given a great deal of attention to industrial promotion.
I have here the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the year 1962, issued over the signature of the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), in which a great deal of attention is paid to the industrial promotions branch. I suggest to all hon. members of the house that it would be very advisable to read the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce, particularly the part dealing with industrial promotion starting at page 27 and running through pages 28, 29 and 30. When they read it they will see that there has been a great deal of emphasis placed on the work of the industrial promotion branch. There is an assistant deputy minister who is in charge, and a great deal of effort and time has been spent in connection with it.
For instance, hon. members will find that inquiries from manufacturers during the last year amounted to over 2,300 as compared to 1,700 the year before. The department goes to great lengths to point out the development which has taken place, the number of exhibitions which have been held, the number of contacts which have been established with manufacturers throughout this country, and the number of contacts established with foreign manufacturers who have been appointing our manufacturers on an agency basis to handle their products. Anybody who reads this report, Mr. Speaker, cannot help but agree that the department has been doing a very efficient job in this connection.
Now, Mr. Speaker, surely making, buying and selling go hand in hand. You cannot make goods without selling them. I suggest very seriously and as emphatically as I can that it is a mistake to divorce these functions of industry. Making, buying and selling should be under one integrated department and not divided, as proposed by this bill, into watertight compartments. I was talking the other day to one of Canada's leading manufacturers. He was telling me about the possibilities of export trade and the necessity of developing it. He said that never once had he sent salesmen abroad at any time without at least their coming back with more than enough orders to pay for the cost of the original


trip, and these orders would be duplicated time and time again. Surely this comes under the aegis of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have our trade commissioners overseas and a most efficient marketing organization. I think it is a real mistake to divorce these departments as now proposed.
I do not think any other countries, certainly any of the major ones of which I have knowledge, have done this. Take, for example, Germany, which is one of the most efficient producing countries in the world, where manufacturing is one of the basic industries which go to the roots of its prosperity. They have a minister of economics dealing with the various functions both of trade and commerce and manufacturing. In the United States, in so far as control comes under the executive-of course a great deal of the control there rests with congress, but so far as control does rest with the executive- there is the secretary of commerce, one minister, who deals with trade and commerce and manufacturing as well.
In the United Kingdom, which as we all know has a long tradition of manufacturing and selling in the markets of the world, there is the board of trade which I think with the exception of shipbuilding and shipping, which come under separate control, covers every other function of industrial development, marketing and commerce. These all come under the control of the president of the board of trade. In France the same situation applies. The minister of finance there has been responsible for the financial and fiscal problems and measures affecting the government of the country. From the beginning the minister of finance had to deal with tariffs. That is not the case in every country. I presume it was the case here, because at one time tariffs went to the very root of the revenue of the country. By far the greater part of our revenue came from customs tariffs, and probably that is the reason, or one of the reasons at any rate, why the minister of finance was in charge of the tariffs. Under our system he is generally in control of the fiscal and financial matters and policies of the government.
As I pointed out at the resolution stage, under a proposal which is now before us on the order paper we will have an economic council set up which will be concerning itself with the planning of economic development, trade, commerce, industry. These matters will come under one minister. Industry will now come under another minister, trade and commerce under another, and then there is finance, the minister of which is supposedly in control of the fiscal and financial problems

of the country. That is four ministers, Mr. Speaker, dealing with this fundamental problem.
I suggest to you, sir, that this is an inefficient way of proceeding, that it is a retrograde step and not one which will aid the development and the industrial life of this country. I believe, as I think we in this party believe, that this bill is thoroughly bad because it will provide for duplication of services. It will provide for duplication of officers, for greater inefficiency of development. It will certainly lead to a greater increase in expansion and will build up a bigger and bigger bureaucracy than ever before.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, for all these reasons we in this party are definitely opposed to the bill. We think it is one which has arisen, perhaps in the same way as many others, from election promises made in the heat of an election campaign. A promise is made to attract attention, and now the government feel it is saddled with its implementation. I suggest with all respect that it will be much better for the government to drop this matter now rather than proceed on this course which I think will lead to inefficiency, and will certainly not promote the industrial development of this counry.

Mr. Speaker, the measure before us has as its stated objective the promotion of industrial well-being in Canada. This is a laudable objective. That has been the policy of my leader, the present Leader of the Opposition, and of his former government during the past six years. The situation facing industry in Canada when we assumed office in 1957 was not encouraging. There was declining industrial activity throughout the country. The St. Lawrence river industrial basin was severely affected. The decline in industrial activity in the mari-times was even more pronounced. The Gordon report on economic development and prospects in Canada recognized and emphasized these facts.
One of the first acts of my leader when his government assumed office in 1957 was to provide annual special grants of approximately $25 million for the maritime provinces because of their special need. This was in keeping with the historic concept of this party, which recognizes the importance and effectiveness of the action taken at the provincial level of government. The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings (Mr. Nowlan), Senator Brooks and the hon. member for Queens (Mr. MacLean), together with a number of others, some of whom are still in this house, were instrumental in bringing these matters to the attention of the government

The national policy of those days was designed to allow for the employment of people through the encouragement of the greatest home building program in Canadian history, a winter works program to assist with municipal development and improvement, vocational training schools, and various aids to institutions such as hospitals, universities, and senior citizens' homes. The measures taken to alleviate the changing conditions confronting the coal mining industry in the maritimes were beneficial, and the present government could have paid them no greater tribute than to renew these particular policies for a further five year period.
The Atlantic development board, proposed during the last parliament, has been adopted by the present administration. Its effectiveness was delayed by the last election campaign. It is noteworthy that the present government would like to claim paternity for this measure although their claims are obviously illegitimate. It will be recalled by hon. members that the Department of Trade and Commerce was revitalized during the period the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Churchill) served as minister. The action taken at that time was to give emphasis to the marketing of Canadian products. The actual implementation of the program conceived at that time was pursued at a later stage in the life of that administration.
I think it is generally agreed in Canada that the emphasis undertaken in that instance was a proper direction in which to promote the well-being of industrial Canada. I view with alarm the obvious desire of the government to interrupt the progress that was taking place along those lines. This bill is a good example of their carelessness regarding our need for markets. I hasten to assure you, sir, that it is not the only one. If hon. members opposite are determined to change something to give effect to the change in name that they have adopted for their party, the most logical and least damaging change that they could make would be in the name of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We on this side of the house would have no objection to changing it to the department of industry and commerce.
This parliament is not concerned with the partisan desires of the present government. The opposition have a duty to perform, and we intend to exercise that prerogative whenever we see the future of this country endangered by that carelessness with which the present government seeks to impose upon our people an enlarged bureaucracy by the establishment of additional departments of government. We on this side of the house are gravely disturbed by the trend that has already been established in this regard. The

Establishment of Industry Department voluntary duplication oi departmental responsibility sought by this careless administration reveals a division of opinion and direction within the present cabinet. We might all be interested, we might even be intrigued by this conflict within the cabinet. However, that is no recommendation for support of this particular bill.
Decisions that were made during the period of world war II and the post-war period have contributed considerably to the problems now facing industry in Canada. The late Hon. C. D. Howe had a great deal to do with establishing the basis for some of these tremendous problems. The demand for goods in Europe following the cessation of hostilities brought with it a tremendous impetus to Canadian industry. It also left the Canadian government of that day with a false sense of security. I can recall the boasts of those days-"You never had it better". The careless attitude of that government can be measured by the budget surpluses of those days. The utter carelessness of that administration in regard to the future is still, even today, one of the most appalling chapters of Canadian history.
The tragedy of those days is to be seen in the unemployment figures of the last 10 years, in the young people who have been denied jobs because of a lack of training. Indeed, it would almost seem that the government of that day thought that the only future for young Canadians was that of common labourer, the pick and shovel for the construction industry, the axe for the timber limits. The bankruptcy of that kind of approach is now well established. The national policy embarked upon during the past six years made provision to overcome this gross carelessness and oversight which had made the reputation of the old Liberal party so distasteful to Canadians.
The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr), who was the first of his race to become minister of labour, was responsible for the introduction of the vocational training building program which was so universally endorsed by the governments of all provinces.
That program was so successful that it has been generally recognized as the most concentrated drive by any government anywhere in the world with respect to the problems of training and instruction to meet changing industrial and labour requirements. The present government has not repudiated that program, and all of us will watch with interest as the benefits accruing from it begin to assert their influence on the industrial scene in Canada.
For these many reasons I am compelled to come back to my contention that the greatest unresolved problem facing industry in Canada is markets. This bill does not begin to grapple


with that problem. I believe this is where we find one of the basic and fundamental differences between those who sit on the government benches and those who sit in the official opposition. I want to emphasize what I said in an earlier debate, that our industrialists are not looking for increased competition brought about by a duplication or multiplication of industrial plants. Their interests and those of Canadian labour are to be found in the implementation of policies and measures that will allow them to become more competitive in world markets as well as those at home. The more intensive utilization of present resources and plant is preferable to a deliberate duplication and multiplication of plants.
The carelessness of this administration in this regard appears to be the most appalling. The failure of the bill to recognize these premises is alarming. The government would be well advised to give this matter further consideration before proceeding with this proposal. I think it is regrettable that the time of parliament should be consumed by this ill disguised partisan gesture which really adds nothing constructive from the point of view of the industrial future of this nation. It is all the more regrettable when consideration is given to the fact that this change of emphasis could very well destroy the trend toward increasing employment which was resulting from the policies brought forward by the previous administration. It is to be hoped that those opposite will forsake their approach and get down to the real business of improving the competitive position of Canadian industry. The best example they can follow in that regard is that which was embarked upon by the previous administration.
The hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings mentioned some of the work that has been embarked upon by the Department of Trade and Commerce during the last several years, and I think it is fair to say that a new concept of the role that department can play in the business and industrial life of this country was adopted during the period when the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre served as minister of that department.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should like to say to hon. members opposite that while the objective set forth in the bill appears to be one that every member of the house can support, in my view the bill will result in a duplication of the services we now have. It will result in an increase in the number of civil servants required, and in the long run it will result in confusion beyond anything we have seen in the past with regard to the production, marketing and distribution of Canadian industrial products.

For this reason I think the government would be well advised to consider the withdrawal of the bill at this time, until they have had an opportunity to consider the matter further.

Mr. Speaker, there are only one or two observations I intend to make in respect of this bill and the general concept that is more and more being shown as characteristic of the new government. I can add very little to the remarks made by the hon. member for Perth and the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, or to the remarks uttered by the hon. member for Rosthern.
However, I think we should look at the general situation that is becoming clearer with the passing days. I refer to the fact that this government has come to the conclusion that as long as it is doing something, what it does must necessarily be effective. The planners are with us, the planners who know what should be done. I am not going to identify them today, but they sit opposite. They have ideas on these questions and they believe they have the answers to all the problems that face the nation. I think they call it directional planning. Well, we have had an example of directional planning in the last few days in the changes, in the declarations and in the retreats that have been made by the government in respect of a measure that is of importance to Canadians.
We find today in every part of this nation the economy is being endangered by the uncertainties that result from planning that was ill digested, ill considered and has had to be changed from day to day. The setting up of this department of government has been an avowed purpose and aim of the Minister of Finance. Indeed, as I look at the plans that are brought before parliament, and others that were set out in the speech from the throne, it becomes more apparent that whatever plans he has are going to be carried into effect by this government, regardless of the consequences.
I am not so sure that there is complete unanimity over there in this regard. I have no reason to be certain in my opinion, but I think some of the more carefully minded members of the government have been somewhat disturbed about the courses of action that are being planned for the Canadian people. I referred to "directional planning". Was it directional planning that only recently brought about a declaration in the budget that has had to be rectified, altered and retreated from? They change from day to day. When we ask them for the latest in the category of change, we cannot get it. The great danger, Mr. Speaker, is that when

There is no part of Canada today that is not suffering because of the uncertainty of this government. Its failure to go through with its so-called plans has not been due to the opposition but has been due to the fact that Canadians as a whole have become mortified at the peripatetic performance of the Minister of Finance and other ministers of this government. I doubt whether in all history the Canadian people, in so short a time, have been so uncertain as to their future as they are today, and so disillusioned by the actions taken by this government. When we ask what is the latest in the catalogue of change the answer is that we must wait; and while parliament waits for the government to decide its course, in every part of this country the economy is being detrimentally affected if not undermined.
The purpose is to increase employment. The objectives referred to by the minister in the course of his speech are laudable in every way. However, even though the objectives of the government are laudable, the means chosen to bring them into effect have proven to be the reverse of the anticipated hopes of the government.
In so far as the setting up of another department is concerned, I am not going into the particulars of the legislation. It will be dealt with clause by clause during the committee stage. However, I do believe it is fair to say that instead of Canada having an expanding economy in consequence of the action taken by this government to date, it is an expensive economy that is being developed in government. They are increasing the number of cabinet ministers, pushing up the stipend of parliamentarians, multiplying the officials in these departments. It is a case of increased bureaucracy and added expense, increased demands upon the taxpayers.
So these people have the idea that the government can do everything. Some time I will deal with that point, Mr. Speaker, and I will name them. I find it difficult to understand, with the number of former civil servants they have in senior positions, why they found it necessary to go outside to get these three wise men. They have the greatest galaxy of former bureaucrats who have ever been gathered together under the aegis of any government. However, they found it necessary to go outside.
This is not going to bring about any expansion. I was interested in this department. It was promised a long while ago by the Minister of Finance. He wrote a book. He

need live in no fear, because when I asked the Prime Minister about it the other day he indicated he had changed his mind. Therefore the cabinet is going to be further enlarged.
Then there are the parliamentary secretaries. I always pay my tribute to young men and women coming into the House of Commons and showing their ability. I could mention a number of them who I know in the years ahead will make great contributions to the country, but strangely enough this government speaks with two voices. There are the ministers and the parliamentary secretaries. To date two of the parliamentary secretaries have spoken and advocated things in the house that are contrary to the views of the cabinet. What did hon. ministers opposite say when we were in office? I refer in particular to the Minister of Justice. He spoke in the house when we set up the Department of Forestry, and he said there should not be any expansion of the cabinet. As recorded at page 5490 of Hansard for June 28, 1960 he said:
May I say to the Prime Minister that it appears to me that the number of ministers is already too high. In that connection a redistribution of functions and responsibilities between these departments would be highly desirable, and that would be met by the suggestion which I have just made.
Then he went on to say:
Too many ministers at the present time. Could that be met by the suggestion which I made earlier that these two services, which are going to be small divisions of this department, should be brought within the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys giving that department the responsibility for the research that you have in mind?
Then he went on to say this, and this is particularly appropriate, because the statement was made in the house on June 28, 1960:
It is obvious that all the ministers in existence today are not needed. I say that to the Prime Minister with deference, because it has been stated here by our members on this side, and in other places, and I do not want to reflect on any private individual; that is why I am very hesitant about replying to the Prime Minister, other than to deal with the question in a general way and say that surely the right hon. gentleman knows there are ministers who are not charged with sufficient duties or sufficient responsibilities. I do not want to go further than that.
That was his view when in opposition. During the election campaign the associate minister of defence was referred to as the fifth wheel, as totally unnecessary. I ask why this promise is not being carried out. Would the cabinet have lost anything by the carrying into effect of this undertaking given during the campaign?

It has been stated that the new minister of this department will also be the Minister of Defence Production. However, that is not my reading of the clause. I cannot go into all the particulars of the clause but I do believe it must be redrafted. If you will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, I wish to refer to clause 8 which states:
In addition to the duties, powers and functions conferred by sections 6 and 7, the minister shall exercise and perform all the duties, powers and functions vested in or required to be exercised and performed by the Minister of Defence Production.
Yet we have an act, and the act is not being amended, which provides that the Department of Defence Production shall have its own minister, who shall receive a salary of $15,000 a year if not occupying another portfolio at the same time. So far as this clause is concerned I suggest it needs to be redrafted.
Regarding the accelerated tendency on the part of the government to get back to the days of an uncontrolled bureaucracy, reference was made by the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Monteith) to two clauses. Clause 11 was one of them, and it goes a long way in the uncontrolled power it seeks to grant. In addition the powers to be given to the minister under clause 7 are very wide, comprehensive and uncontrolled. There is no control over them in any way. Legislative authority is being given to the minister to do almost anything. The clause reads:
The minister shalldevelop and carry out such programs and projects as may be appropriate
(i) to assist the adaptation of manufacturing industries to changing conditions in domestic and exports markets-
That is a very wide power. It gives him the power to act, when joined with the power of the governor in council, and do almost anything that he chooses to do, provided he can get the cabinet to agree and without regard to parliament.
Clause 11 reads:
The governor in council may authorize and direct departments, branches and agencies of the government of Canada to undertake in the execution of their respective duties and functions such special measures as may be appropriate to facilitate the economic development of any designated area or the adjustment of industry in that area.
Never in my experience in the days of peace, with the exception of the Defence Production Act, have such powers been granted to a minister. There is no control over the governor in council; he can bring in special measures to facilitate the economic development of any designated area or the adjustment of industry in that area, and he does not have to come to parliament for authority. Under this clause the governor in

That is a tremendous power. Even under a socialist government in the province of Saskatchewan, often criticized, that power has never been exceeded. There were two or three departments of government in those days whose deputy ministers are today ministers of the crown in the present cabinet. We thought we were past the threat of the exercise of such powers following the pipe line debate of 1956.
It looks simple on the face of it, Mr. Speaker; but read it. Clause 11 constitutes as nearly as possible a complete abdication by parliament of its rights. Are we going to hand the governor in council the right to determine what special measures shall be carried out? Are we going to give him the power to adjust industry in any area? The adjustment of industry in any area is a matter within the legislative competence of the provincial government concerned. Let that be clear. Hear, hear.

There are many more criticisms that could be offered in respect of this measure, Mr. Speaker. There is the shuffling around from one department to another. We have an example of it in the Department of Agriculture. That Department had authority over the wheat board and over the marketing of wheat, and we sold our wheat while it had that authority. Why proliferate these agencies of government, these departments? Mr. Speaker, I am opposed to this legislation while agreeing with its objectives. My first reason for being opposed to it is that there is no possible justification for increasing the size of this cabinet and, in consequence, the number of the officials necessary to make it operative. Second, there is no reason why the Department of Trade and Commerce could not discharge these responsibilities. This is simply the age old experience of bureaucracy multiplying like rabbits; that is what it amounts to. Expand, bring in new departments, give more authority; the more departments you have-this has been the experience of anybody who has had responsibility in public life-the more desire on the part of those in that department to spend money in order to justify the existence of the department and the responsibilities they discharge. I presume that is the reason the Prime Minister said he was going to rid this country of the associate minister of national defence. Well, he has not done it. Instead of reducing, they increase.
I am not going to deal with the bifurcation of the Department of Agriculture because that matter will be raised at another time. But I would like to know how two ministers with the same powers and the same responsibilities are going to carry on. I think the present Minister of Agriculture will be the senior, because he has a compelling personality. It will be just too bad for the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Tremblay). This is all part and parcel-and I speak very seriously now-of planners planning to pretend they are doing something and thereby being able to say "See what we have done in the first 68 days". This planning, the establishment of this department with the powers that are contained in this bill, cannot but strengthen the authority of bureaucracy and give to those who are charged with the responsibility the power to push Canadians around. It would perhaps be desirable for me to try to cover on clause 1 some of the points which were raised on second reading but which were not replied to. These will be in the nature of general remarks in answer to specific references.
The hon. member for Perth indicated that he felt some apprehension that this bill was another manifestation of what he called a tendency of the government to take over in a socialist way the entire economy. If the hon. member would read the bill carefully he would see, I think, that the powers of the minister are very limited in extent. There is a definition of his duties, but his powers are not of a character which would be likely to bring about a situation of the kind which the hon. member for Perth envisaged.
The hon. member was also apprehensive about the possibility, or likelihood, of disputes arising between the federal and the provincial governments inasmuch as the provinces clearly have a responsibility in relation to industrial matters within their own provinces, as does the federal government in relation to industry generally within Canada. A similar situation has arisen with regard to other federal government departments, the Department of Agriculture, for example, which has duplicates in each of the provinces. It has been found that given a degree of consultation and co-operation, conflicts do not arise.

I suggest to the hon. member for Perth that this will be the approach of the new ministry of industry-to recognize that there are tasks to be undertaken, some of which can more appropriately be done by the provinces and others which can be best performed by the federal government; some of these are currently being carried out to a limited degree by the Department of Trade and Commerce here in Ottawa.
The purpose of this new ministry is to intensify, extend and make more effective the work which has hitherto been performed within the Department of Trade and Commerce under the aegis of one of the assistant deputy ministers.
The hon. member for Perth also made a suggestion that the purpose accomplished by this bill could have been accomplished equally well by renaming the Department of Trade and Commerce and leaving it substantially as it is. One of his hon. friends, I think it was the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, made the same suggestion, but recognizing that this idea would probably not v/ork, he advanced gradually in the course of his argument to the point where he acknowledged it might be advisable to appoint a deputy minister within the department as a deputy minister for industry. To my way of thinking this was implicit acknowledgment of the necessity of having someone with greater scope, greater stature, than an assistant deputy minister to carry out the functions which should be performed in this field. This is precisely what we propose to provide.
This measure does, also, have the effect of putting the functions now being performed within the Department of Trade and Commerce alongside those of the Department of Defence Production. That department is at present much more intimately concerned with manufacturing in Canada today than is the non-industrial side of the Department of Trade and Commerce whose gaze is, naturally, turned outward and concerned with assisting Canadians to participate in external markets. Because of this, the functions of the present Department of Trade and Commerce are to some extent divided between external considerations and domestic or internal considerations. By removing these internal functions in relation to manufacturing industry and transferring them to the new department it will be possible to link them closely with the domestic operations of the Department of Defence Production and provide for a more effective integration of the skills within the government, bringing them into play to assist industry in Canada. More could be achieved in this way than by simply renaming the Department of Trade and Commerce the Department of Industry and Commerce and letting it go at that.

But, as I say, it has the consequence that in respect of a given unit of output fewer human muscles are called for. This is a dilemma of which the government is acutely aware and a problem which will have to preoccupy to a large degree the new

I think the hon. member also raised the question of the reorganization of the Department of Trade and Commerce, with the provision of a separate deputy minister within that department for industrial matters. As I suggested earlier, I am sure that if a group, a section or a department under a deputy minister is necessary and desirable- and, like him, I feel that it is-a better place or a better linkage of association for such a department or deputy minister is in conjunction or in association with the Department of Defence Production, which is already to a very large degree intensively involved with the heavy manufacturing industries of Canada.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond, while in favour of establishing the new department, suggested that perhaps the occasion might be taken to abolish the Department of Defence Production. As a consequence of this it would be possible to effect an economy of some 1,520 civil servants. While measures of economy I think are always desirable and certainly are always looked into, I should point out that the establishment of a new department of industry will in no wise lessen the necessity for carrying out and continuing to carry out the present purchasing and development functions now being carried on by the Department of Defence Production. Somebody will still have to do this work, and merely abolishing the department and disestablishing its staff will not make it possible to continue the work being done. As I mentioned earlier, it is intended to make use of the services, skills and knowledge related to manufacturing industry now extant within the Department of Defence Production, and bring these into play in the most extensive way possible in order to avoid the duplication of building up a duplicate staff in the department of industry which would merely overlap with the present knowledge and skills in the Department of Defence Production. I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond will agree that unless we abolish our armed forces, which is unlikely, it will not be possible to abolish the Department of Defence Production.

I have never seen it or read of it in any of the writings for which the government has been responsible. Mr. Chairman, in his earlier remarks the minister, in answering the question which has been raised previously about cutting down on the Department of Trade and Commerce and transferring its functions to the new department, attempted to make out a case for a closer connection-as I understood him; and I do not want to misquote him at all-between the Department of Defence Production and industry than exists between the Department of Trade and Commerce and industry. I am not satisfied that this is the case. I was talking yesterday about weakening the Department of Trade and Commerce by cutting out from it a large and effective branch now called domestic commerce under an assistant deputy minister, with four branches underneath that, the standards branch, the industrial promotion branch, the small business branch and the industrial design branch, all of which have a direct bearing on industry in Canada.
My argument was that we have, in effect, functioning a department able to do the work which is suggested for the proposed new department. I consider it is a mistake to disrupt the organized work of the Department of Trade and Commerce by creating this new department of industry, which involves drawing away from the Department of Trade and Commerce some of the skilled and capable personnel who are already there, breaking a link between industry and that department which has already been strongly established, and trying to set it up again. Here you will have a new minister, a new deputy minister and a new department starting more or less from scratch making contact with industry and determining what are the requirements

for government assistance to industry. The minister indicated, I thought, that the Department of Defence Production has a closer link with industry than has the Department of Trade and Commerce, and I question that very much.
What does the Department of Defence Production do? It gets its instructions from the Department of National Defence. I remember the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe telling us here years ago that the Department of Defence Production simply carried out the instructions from the Department of National Defence. That was when he made the famous statement that if they wanted a gold plated piano, the Department of Defence Production would have to procure it for them. But what does the Department of Defence Production do? It allocates the orders to fulfil the requirements of the Department of National Defence, and of course it comes in contact with a large number of industrial concerns in Canada. In the estimates for the fiscal year 1963-64 for the Department of National Defence, under the heading of procurements, adding together the three services there is a placement of orders amounting to about $300 million. In the Department of Defence Production's estimates there is an allotment of $10 million for development projects. Therefore to that extent the Department of Defence Production has a link with industry in the country. However, as I pointed out yesterday when quoting figures from the dominion bureau of statistics, there are in Canada almost 37,000 establishments in the field of manufacturing and the gross value of products in 1959 was $23 billion. That may be quite a bit higher now; I have not the latest figures. So the Department of Defence Production is only touching a segment of the industrial framework of Canada, whereas the Department of Trade and Commerce ranges over the whole field and has contact with industrial establishments and the manufacturing industry right across this country.
That was the purpose some years ago-I think it was in 1957 or 1958-of our establishing the small business branch within the Department of Trade and Commerce, to make contact with the thousands of small businesses across the country. This is a much more wide-ranging contact with industry than has the Department of Defence Production. I do not suggest that the Department of Defence Production is not doing good work with industry, and certainly with heavy industry, but there are other departments which similarly have contacts with industry in this country. The Department of Public Works is constantly letting out contracts for one thing and another; certainly it has a great interest 28902-5-1081

My argument yesterday, and I continue it today, is that this is a mistake, in that a very strong department, trade and commerce-which could be called industry and commerce-is being weakened by this proposal. As the Leader of the Opposition pointed out this morning, this idea arose, apparently, some years ago, in the mind of the present Minister of Finance. His program, enunciated in some of his writings, has now been placed before parliament without a careful consideration of parliamentary procedure and the methods by which government is carried on in this country. The hon. gentleman

I would not agree with it in the way in which it is phrased. The ideal, obviously, would be to have an industrial structure which employs everybody who is seeking a job, even at the expense of some efficiency in the production of goods and services in terms of cost. Unfortunately, if one, by reason of employing too many individuals and too little in the way of automation, allows costs to rise, the demand for those goods is diminished. It is demand which is the

In the export and import field one has to consider not only commodities but the invisible items, such as the tourist trade, freight, shipping and assorted monetary payments such as dividends, interest and the flow of capital. So what one would hope for is that we would be able to move as rapidly as possible to a position of balance in respect of our total payments. In so far as we are committed, and are likely to be for some time, to a net deficit in respect of interest and dividends, this means that some of this deficit has to be made up by a favourable balance in respect of commodities, tourist and freight.

I think perhaps the simple answer would be that there already exists in the federal government a number of departments whose concern is either the raw material itself or the extractive process. In the case of forest products there is the Department of Forestry which is concerned with the production of the raw materials of the forest products industry. It is less concerned with the intensive processing of these products beyond the more or less elementary stage, and it is in this secondary stage or what is known as secondary industry that the concern and interest of the department of industry will arise and the interest of the Department of Forestry will stop. He said: This bill which I am proposing today, Mr. Speaker, is the same bill as the one I moved during the last session. In my opinion, the bill deals with the same general principle as all the other bills which have been introduced by members of the house dealing with the general question of interest rates. I had hoped that this bill, along with the other bills, would have been referred to the committee on banking for its consideration. However, since that has not been agreed to, I propose to discuss the subject matter today.
The necessity for this bill arises basically because the people of Canada simply do not

Know how much it costs to borrow money. They could find out very easily how much it would cost to buy a car or a television set, but clearly the ordinary person does not know how much money costs him. The price of money is never expressed in language that 99 per cent of the public could possibly understand. It is easy to borrow money for a dollar down and a dollar a week or so much per month, but finding out what the real annual interest rate is is about as difficult as pulling teeth.
It is quite common, for instance, for working people to borrow $8 when they go to work on Monday morning on the promise that they will pay back $10 on Friday when they get paid. There are many people who do this who have no idea of the agreement which has been made. In fact, the rate of interest on this transaction would be about 1,825 per cent a year.
Because it is easy to borrow money-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: May I interrupt the hon. member? Is he discussing Bill No. C-10 or Bill No. C-12?

I am discussing Bill No. C-12, Mr. Speaker. The reason I am talking about interest rates is my feeling that people get in over their heads partly because they do not know what the interest rates are. I will come to the essential principles of Bill No. C-12 before I conclude my remarks. It is so easy to borrow money because we have all become accustomed to trying to live to the standard of our neighbours. It is practically a sin not to own a car, not to have a television set, not to have a washing machine and dryer, and not to own one's own house. More and more, people are borrowing money or buying merchandise on time. Most reputable retailers encourage instalment buying. Most proper finance companies practically roll out the red carpeting for people who come in to use their services or borrow money. Of course, they all hide the exorbitant rate of interest which they charge.
If anyone doubts that, all he has to do is look at the statement made by the Canadian retail federation to the royal commission on banking and finance, which spells out their stand on what we ought to do about interest rates. They refer to the proposals which have been made in this house and in other chambers to the effect that the actual interest rate should be spelled out. They say that this kind of proposal is mischievous nonsense; that such knowledge would be misleading, confusing, incorrect and unworkable. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, the only thing unworkable about it would be that the retailers might sell a little less merchandise. I had never heard such a completely selfish attitude on the part of any group in this society, until I heard that.
Bankruptcy Act
I do not question the need for consumer credit because such credit has helped us raise our standard of living, provide material comforts for many people. It has increased production and it has helped to create jobs. However, we have had too many instances of tremendous hardship as a result of the excessive use of credit. These hardships have been created, in part at least, as a result of lack of knowledge of the interest rate charged and partly by pressure to conform with our neighbours. An interesting memorandum was prepared recently by the federation of national trade unions. They give a concrete example of the kind of difficulty into which people get. I want to read from the memorandum, Mr. Speaker.
Here is a case of a union member who bought $1,900 worth of merchandise on terms. The merchant boosted his price by from 40 per cent to 50 per cent in order to give a supposed exchange allowance and to legalize the deal. The result was an interest rate not of 27 per cent, but of at least 60 per cent. This union member has been in debt to the same company for 12 years, yet he really owns nothing because the company has a bond on all the furniture. This man purchased a washer and dryer, and then fell victim to a thorough exploitation on the system of exchanging. The real value of the two pieces of merchandise he bought was $600, but because a sewing machine was exchanged on the deal he was charged $858. He was allowed $383 as a credit on the sewing machine, and the actual allowance on the sewing machine was really $125. It had been purchased for $464, had only been used for six months, and the company resold it for $400. This left a profit on the deal to the company of $275, plus the profit on the financing, plus the profit on the sale of the washer and dryer.
The same man purchased a bedroom set from the company. The regular retail price of the bedroom set was $385, which was double the wholesale price. However, it was invoiced to the man at $579, which leaves a surcharge of $194 over the regular price. Then, $200 was allowed on a used bedroom set which, according to information supplied to the man, was later resold for at least $100. The balance owing, after the deduction of the allowance, was $397.95. This amount, financed at a basic rate of 27 per cent, gives an interest income of $107, plus $100 exploitation in the exchange deal, which makes a hidden interest rate of about 60 per cent.
Moreover, the law states that upon any refinancement, the merchant retains his bond on all merchandise covered by previous contracts. So, we have here the case of a family which had been refinancing for 12 years.

Bankruptcy Act
There have been six refinancements paid with the well known penalty of approximately 30 per cent, and that is why, after 12 years, they still owe the company $3,148.25; and I may say this man has a salary of $60 a week.
I have spoken about how easy it is to get credit. According to the Bank of Canada, loans to consumers went up by $300 million from 1957 to 1960. The difficulties arise not in the borrowing of the money but after a person has borrowed money or purchased goods. This is when his difficulties begin.
Often the trouble comes not from the retailer, who is usually friendly, but from some finance company to which the retailer has sold the paper, as it is called in the trade. How difficult it can be for a person is illustrated in a news report which appeared in the Montreal Star on Wednesday June 19 last. I shall only quote a portion of it. The heading of the report reads, "Collection Agency to Pay Damages." It states:
A Superior Court judge yesterday labelled as reprehensible and illegal the action of a collection agency and a bailiff in breaking down the door of a supposed debtor and seizing his furniture.
Further on it states:
The judge said that on one occasion two men forced their way into the house in St. Michel and evaluated the furniture and that on another occasion, when the man and wife attempted to barricade themselves to protect their property, their door was broken down with an axe and the furniture seized.
This is an extreme case; but there are thousands of cases where people have difficulties with threatening letters, telephone calls, personal calls at their door at all times of the day and night, garnishee orders and lost jobs. These troubles are common to people finding themselves in the position of having to buy on credit, and by that time people are so far in debt that they cannot pay their bills even if they wished.
The bill in my name would add a new clause to the Bankruptcy Act. It would permit the insolvent wage earner to make an assignment to a trustee appointed by the courts. The wage earner would submit his wages to the trustee, who would make regular payments, on the order that the wage earner could afford, to the creditors. Where the contract signed by the wage earner is unconscionable, then the courts could exempt the wage earner from payment of excessive interest charges. The courts could also enforce obedience to the arrangements worked out by the trustee, and would have power to discharge the wage earner when he has fulfilled his obligations.
Bills similar to this have been enacted in the United States where they have helped
[Mr. Orlikow.l
thousands of people. The bill would help not only the wage earner but the legitimate creditor. It would help the wage earner by taking inordinate pressure off him and permitting orderly payment of his debts. It would also help the legitimate creditor because he would be more likely to get his money.
I had hoped this bill would be submitted along with other bills to the committee on banking and commerce, but since that has not been agreed upon, I hope hon. members will discuss the basic principles involved, will realize the importance of this subject, have a full sense of the tremendous hardship experienced by many people, and that they will not talk the bill to death so that it will die on the order paper at six o'clock.
