Mr. Speaker, I think that Bill C-12 just introduced by the hon. member has some justification, because it is based upon quite acceptable motives.
However, while the bill's mover was speaking, I was wondering whether he was referring to Bill C-10, an act to amend the Interest Act, or Bill C-12, an act to amend the Bankruptcy Act.
The bill proposed by the hon. member raises rather serious problems for a member from the province of Quebec.
In the first place, Mr. Speaker, I notice that, to my way of thinking, Bill C-12 is interfering with something about which Quebec is extremely sensitive, especially these days where new constitutional problems have arisen. In my opinion Bill C-12 intervenes in a field where Quebec has already legislated. If the federal government was in a position to intervene in this provincial matter through a bankruptcy act, I feel it is because the constitution enabled the central government to intervene with regard to commercial matters.
However, Bill No. C-12 aims at protecting the employees' rights and not the merchants'.
Mr. Speaker, I consider it an interference in the civil law of the province of Quebec and I feel it would be unconstitutional to adopt Bill No. C-12, because it intervenes in the field of civil law. I maintain that the civil law of the province of Quebec must be jealously guarded by that province, as stipulated in the constitution.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that too often unlucky wage earners have assumed obligations for years to come and are obliged today to pay back interest or debts for years before they can free themselves. I agree that

something should be done for those people, but the provinces can do it, and the province of Quebec has taken steps in that field.
We have, in the province of Quebec, what is called the Lacombe act, which has been incorporated in the civil code to cover such cases. That legislation authorizes, for instance, a debt-ridden wage earner who cannot meet his liabilities, to go to the clerk's office at the magistrate's court and make a declaration to the effect that he is unable to pay his debts.
At that time, he gives to the clerk the list of his creditors who are then advised by the clerk himself; and, each week, according to the provisions of the Lacombe act, the debtor who is unable to meet his liabilities is obliged to pay a certain amount according to his means, which amount is set by law; it is not left to the discretion of a judge, but is determined by law. A married wage earner may take $24 off his pay for himself, and has to pay 30 per cent on the balance. A married wage earner who makes $84 a week keeps $24; while having to pay 30 per cent on the remaining $60 to the clerk of the magistrate's court, that is $18. The difference between $84 and $18 which represents his own salary, he uses to meet his current obligations, and not his past liabilities.
If the individual is unmarried and earns $84 a week, the clerk deducts $12, while keeping $21.60 of the balance of $72 to pay the creditors.
Every third month, the clerk distributes to the creditors the accumulated money in proportion to the amount of the claim they have against this hapless debtor.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that this act, in the province of Quebec, meets the objects of Bill C-12 moved by the hon. member. A close study of the bill shows that there are some points which, in my opinion, even though they were to be implemented would not be practical in the province of Quebec.
I understand that Bill No. C-12 has very commendable objects, but for instance, if we take subclause 2 of clause 26(b) which reads as follows:
The trustee may apply to the court for relief in respect of any executory contract; and, after hearing upon notice, when the court finds that, having regard to the risk and to all the circumstances, the financial obligations under the contract upon the wage earner are excessive or that the obligations generally are harsh and unconscionable,
The clause also stipulates that the court may intervene. Now, in accordance with the civil code of the province of Quebec, both
Bankruptcy Act
criterias mentioned in subclause 2 of clause 26(b) cannot apply, and I mean the risk and other circumstances.
According to the civil code of the province of Quebec, a judge cannot intervene in a contract unless he can ascertain that excessive harshness has been suffered by the debtor. The judge can intervene only when the party is a person under age and this is confirmed in section 1,001 of the civil code of the province of Quebec.
In the province of Quebec, according to French law, the judge may intervene in a contract only under definite conditions, such as an error in the essence of the contract, either by fraudulent practices, violence or fear.
Mr. Speaker, I think that subclause 2 of clause 26(b) could not be enacted in the province of Quebec, because it does not meet the spirit of the law. In that province, a contract is either legal or illegal. If it is legal, it is entirely so, and the judge cannot modify one clause or another. It is either good or bad. It is impossible to intervene, because, according to French civil law, a contract expresses the will of both parties in writing; or, if it is a commercial agreement, it must be expressed so as to give proof thereof. Therefore, sub-clause 2 of clause 26(b) could not in practice apply to the province of Quebec. As I mentioned earlier today, this would be completely outside the usual framework of law administration.
Now, there is a point I would like to raise. Under clause 26(b), subclause 1, the hon. member suggests that a trustee may be a responsible person without necessarily being an authorized trustee. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with it because it is already difficult enough to find competent trustees to administer the assets of a bankrupt. If anybody who has not the least idea of the law were asked to administer the assets and property of a bankrupt, we would have chaos and would be unable to find any solution. This would render the administration of the law still more complicated than it is now.
Mr. Speaker, while we are discussing the Bankruptcy Act, I must say that I am opposed to the concept of the mover of the bill which asks people-practically anybody- to look after the Bankruptcy Act. I think, Mr. Speaker, that too many trustees do not know the act and especially in the province of Quebec where the problem is even more difficult because this act has a British background. I mean it is an English act proceeding from English philosophy. We, in the

Bankruptcy Act
province of Quebec, have the French civil code and it is extremely difficult, Mr. Speaker, to reconcile in practice the provisions of the Bankruptcy Act with the practice and the civil code of the province of Quebec because the two acts proceed from completely different philosophies.
Mr. Speaker, instead of entrusting the implementation of the Bankruptcy Act to people even less qualified, I suggest that we should find more qualified people who know the act better than those who carry it out at the present time and they are numerous among the trustees. I think that the director of the bankruptcy division should enforce some kind of regulations to compel people to know our legislation a little better because in the province of Quebec, the conflict between those two acts is extreme. Furthermore, it raises many problems which are very difficult for our courts to settle.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, I am in agreement with the principle of the bill, that seeks to help people in financial difficulties. But I object to this bill being passed by the house because once again it interferes, especially in the province of Quebec, with the civil code which we want to preserve preciously in the province of Quebec.
Many provisions in this bill are in direct contradiction with the spirit of our legislation. I say that this is an area where the federal government must intervene with the utmost caution, because the Bankruptcy Act is applicable in the case of businessmen. Under Bill C-12, we are infringing upon the civil code of the province of Quebec, and I am convinced that we should not go forward with it because we must respect it as provided by the Canadian constitution and the B.N.A. Act, that is that the civil law comes under the exclusive jurisdiction of the province of Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the remarks of the sponsor of Bill C-12, as well as the comments just made on the subject.
I also feel bound to express a certain fear, like my friend, about the possible infringement of this bill on our provincial legislation.
On the other hand, as our friend pointed out with some alarm, we actually have a federal Bankruptcy Act which applies in the province of Quebec and the implementation of the provisions of this new bill would not succeed in solving our constitutional problems. But at this point, it is still not the main cause for concern. I would rather be in favour of referring the bill to a committee that would settle the constitutional issue.

It is true that in the province of Quebec we have the Lacombe act, but it is a dreadful act for the poor debtor. The Lacombe act favours the bad guy, the large creditor who tempts the customer with things which are above the latter's financial means, makes him sign a finance contract which the purchaser cannot afford-as the mover of the bill pointed out-and afterwards grabs the debtor by the throat. It is really the Lacombe act which takes debtors by the throat since, before they are through, they have to pay back two and even three times the amount they owe. The legal fees double and triple the amount of the debt.
I am in favour of the principle of the bill, but that does not mean that we should adopt it since the point in question is whether those finance contracts are legal or not, as someone said a while ago.
This is why I believe that the bill should not be carried in its present wording. But nevertheless, it was fitting to present it, if only to draw the attention of provincial authorities on the necessity of protecting debtors against those loan sharks, who well deserve such a name. In fact, they systematically take unfair advantage of the borrower who does not know how and to what extent he is committed, believing that he will be in a position to meet the weekly instalments of $2, $5 or $10, but unfortunately he is unable to do so.
Then he comes under the Lacombe act for five years, maybe ten. I do not think that is right. I think it would be unfair to force a person to pay a debt he incurred, perhaps through some misfortune, within a three-year period, as provided in the bill.
That is why I am opposed to the bill, but I congratulate the mover for submitting the idea. I do hope provincial governments will use it to ensure that there will be a greater amount of justice in finance enterprises. (Text):

While I realize that the sponsor of this bill is trying to arrive at some solution of the difficulties he has mentioned I feel that in presenting this measure in its present form he is creating more problems than the bill itself would solve.
We have heard him for two thirds of the time during which he spoke talk about unconscionable transactions. I do not think this bill is designed to deal with that subject. The hon. member is trying, in this proposed amendment to The Bankruptcy Act, to deal

with the situation of a person of small means who cannot afford to go bankrupt under the present regulations of the act, the man who cannot make an assignment because he cannot pay a trustee.
Hon. members who have spoken so far seem to think that the man who will be involved in these situations is the man who has run into some ogre of a department store or other concern which has led him down the garden path. I reject that entirely. Certainly, there are persons who get into trouble because they have entered into unconscionable transactions; but there are also many men and women who have got into financial difficulties out of sheer stupidity, carelessness or wanton spending. Let us not say they are all to be pitied. Account should be taken, too, of the honest traders with whom these people deal-the service station operator whose bills for tires and gasoline are not paid; the tailor from whom they buy suits or dresses; the doctor; the dentist.
As I said, I think this bill creates more problems than it solves. We know that some years ago in Manitoba there was a provincial act, unfortunately declared ultra vires, which made some progress in dealing with these problems. There was a parallel act in Ontario which also fell by the wayside because of the doubt which was cast on the act in Manitoba. It is one I have been interested in as far as Alberta is concerned, because I believe we have there a mechanism for reaching a solution, if we can make appropriate amendments to The Bankruptcy Act. Under these provisions the provincial authority would be empowered to name some public authority which might without a fee, make assignments on behalf of creditors. We have set up informally a debtors assistance board in Alberta to which a man might come and make a proposal for settling his affairs. Unfortunately, it sometimes happens that when he begins to pay out, one of the creditors hearing of the arrangement may say: This will take too long; this man is now earning some money so I will garnishee his wages. Well, we know what happens in most instances when this is done. The employer simply says: We cannot be bothered with this; you had better leave our employ. Thus the greedy creditor has eliminated any source of relief for the remaining creditors.
I have worked closely with this debtors assistance board. We have seen people there who really should not have gone bankrupt. They have needed help to sort out their debts
Bankruptcy Act
-someone who would bring the creditors together in an informal way and help them to hammer out a proposal whereby, voluntarily, they would pay a certain sum on a regular basis, allowing the creditors to get a reasonable share while enabling the debtors to live. That is what we have aimed at.
I do not think this amendment to the Bankruptcy Act will achieve that purpose. As a previous speaker has indicated, to have some local official or court set aside obligations, or to rank secured obligations, will fly in the face of other legislation both provincial and federal. I would say it would be unconstitutional and ultra vires. We know numbers of people who are in trouble financially and who are purchasing homes with the assistance of direct loans from the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. How on earth could we under this legislation simply authorize a court to set aside the terms of the mortgage? It would make nonsense of provincial legislation as well as of property and of civil rights, especially where our mortgage regulations are governed, as they are in Alberta, by provincial law.
I do not share the constitutional worries of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Girouard) or of the hon. member for St. Maurice-La-fleehe (Mr. Chretien), that for some reason or other the national bankruptcy law is an intrusion on provincial jurisdiction and is designed for commercial operations only. I have never known that the Bankruptcy Act was so limited. A man may be a wage earner or self-employed; he can still qualify for the protection afforded by the Bankruptcy Act. It is said that bankruptcy legislation constitutes an intrusion into provincial civil law, that there is a different mentality in the province of Quebec with respect to civil law. Is there to be a different criminal law for that province? Is there a different mentality in the province in that respect, and should there be a different system of administration of justice? I am afraid I cannot share that opinion. If we have a bankruptcy law it should apply from one end of the country to the other. But I do feel that trying to make an amendment to the bankruptcy law, as this bill seeks to do, is not a practical course of conduct. The result of this proposed legislation would be to play ducks and drakes with provincial laws enacted under appropriate provincial jurisdiction, and to me that is quite wrong.
I would prefer to have the hon. member spend more time endeavouring to show how wage earners or persons of limited means could be assisted by way of a wage earner's

Bankruptcy Act
assignment. I think some parts of the bill are quite workable, but in the form proposed I think it would create far more problems than it would solve. The bill says that a trustee shall be paid 5 per cent of the sums to be handled by him. I think it would be far better however if an appropriate amendment were made to the Bankruptcy Act whereby provincial authorities could set up a quasi public body which would handle the administration of the small debtors' debts. This would do everyone a service, not only the debtor but also the creditor, who has rights too.

Mr. Speaker, when the proposer of this bill first rose to his feet he raised some question in this house as to why the bill would not be referred, as would others dealing with the control of consumer credit, to the proposed joint committee of this house and the Senate at such time as the committee is established to deal with this subject. In opening my remarks this afternoon I should like to point out, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has already said, that in essence this bill achieves two separate objectives. First, it provides an amendment to the Bankruptcy Act to carry into federal law the former provisions of a number of western statutes which made provision for the orderly payment of debts, and also attempts to carry into federal law, under the guise of bankruptcy, the provisions of what was in Ontario up until last year the unconscionable transactions relief act.
In my view the reason this bill should not be referred to the joint committee on consumer credit, when this committee is established, is that the terms of reference of that committee would not provide for an appropriate discussion of bankruptcy legislation. Hon. members will perhaps recall that a bill dealing with substantially the same subject matter was passed in the other place last session and introduced into this house, receiving first reading on January 21, 1963. There is at the present time a bill substantially in the form of that bill under the aegis of the government now before the other place. While agreeing generally with the comments of the hon. gentleman with regard to the desirability of setting up some procedure to provide for the orderly payment of debts, my position this afternoon would be that I think that that legislation, when it comes forward, would be a much more desirable means of achieving this end, and I would say that further consideration of this bill should be deferred until this legislation can be brought forward.
[Mr. Lambert.)
In view of the comments which have been made by some hon. gentlemen this afternoon with regard to the constitutionality of the provisions of this bill, I think it might be of some assistance briefly to pursue the legislative pedigree of this proposed legislation. A Manitoba statute called the orderly payment of the debts act was first introduced into that province by the Manitoba legislature in 1932. This statute apparently was a success and commended itself to the legislature of the native province of the hon. member for Edmonton West, which in 1959 enacted a statute substantially in the same form. Some question was raised at that time before the statute had been proclaimed, as to the constitutionality of its provisions, and a reference was made by the lieutenant governor in council of that province, first to the appellate division of the supreme court of Alberta, and then to the Supreme Court of Canada, which ultimately determined that that form of statute was substantially a matter in pith and substance concerning bankruptcy and insolvency, a subject matter which is conferred on the federal government by section 91 of the British North America Act. It was following that adverse decision with regard to the Alberta legislation, which of course provided a declaratory statement with respect to the constitutionality of the Manitoba legislation, that the attorneys general of those two provinces, as I understand it, requested action be taken by the federal government. The previous government took steps to prepare a bill, which was Bill No. S-2 in the last session and is Bill No. S-2 in this session.
There was a second motivation behind the federal government's action at that time. Hon. members will perhaps be familiar with the provisions of the present Bankruptcy Act, which were first introduced in 1949, regarding summary administration of estates. Those provisions provided what was felt to be a simpler and less expensive course of action for dealing with bankrupt estates, where the debtor's total assets were not in excess of $500. The summary administration provisions of the Bankruptcy Act have, in the judgment of most persons knowledgeable in this field, proven to be unsatisfactory, and therefore it was proposed that immediate action should be taken by way of this bill not only to enact a procedure for the orderly payment of debts but also to dispose of the unsatisfactory summary administration proceedings.
I should like at this point to make reference in detail to two objections I have to the hon. member's bill. I refer to the terms of section 26b (1), in which we learn that the

wage earner in a particular case is to commence proceedings by making an assignment. I would point out to all hon. members that the consequence of that under the existing terms of the Bankruptcy Act is that the wage earner will have committed an act of bankruptcy. It is my understanding that the objective of the provincial legislation and the objective of the whole legislative scheme is that an honest, responsible wage earner should be entitled by this procedure, by means of a consolidation order, to avoid the stigma of bankruptcy. Yet the hon. member, under the terms of his bill, makes it mandatory that the debtor should take the bankruptcy proceedings.
Further difficulties arise from this. As a result of committing an act of bankruptcy, what effect does the action of filing an assignment have on the other provisions of the Bankruptcy Act? In particular, what if the debtor falls behind in his payments? What if further and other capital assets, as opposed to earnings, of the debtor are later discovered? How are they to be applied within the terms of the Bankruptcy Act, and how are they to be applied to the debt? Unfortunately, Bill No. C-12 is silent on all these points. The hon. member for St. Maurice-Lafleche (Mr. Chretien) has already pointed out the disadvantage of proceeding by way of appointment of a trustee, and not even a licensed trustee at that, in order to administer the provisions.
One of the difficulties of the current summary administration provisions of the Bankruptcy Act has been not only the difficulty of securing a reliable trustee, but substantial evidence has been presented of a number of abuses in respect of these summary administration provisions. Here the hon. member would not only not require the basic requirement of licensing so as to establish a person's financial responsibility and professional ability, but he would permit the assignment to be made to a person who had not even sustained those preliminary standards. This I feel would be a defect in the proceeding. This is one of the provisions with regard to which I think the bill before the Senate involving the terms of the Manitoba and Alberta statutes is superior to this particular piece of legislation. Under those provisions no trustee or person acting in the role of trustee is required. Rather, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has pointed out, an officer of the county or district court in the appropriate province is the person to whom the assignment is made. He is the person who is responsible for carrying out the administration of the consolidation order.
The hon. member has devoted most of his time in making his remarks on this subject
Bankruptcy Act
to the provisions of clause 26b (2) which, as I have already pointed out, reincorporates substantially the terms of the unconscionable transactions relief act of Ontario which was declared ultra vires and void in the province of Ontario by the court of appeal of that province in late 1962. It would be inappropriate, I think, for hon. members to discuss the provisions of that particular statute in parliament at this time because the decision of the Ontario court of appeal is now under appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada and is awaiting hearing. It would be contrary to the rules of the house to do that.
With regard to the provisions concerning interest let me simply say that I feel it would be premature for action or even discussion on this subject not only in this house but in a committee of this house, as the hon. member has suggested. I also think it would be much more appropriate to deal with these particular procedures by way of a separate bill, if the hon. member felt it was necessary, so that the bill could be referred to the committee on consumer credit.
I should like to point out that one of the motives of the government in introducing Bill No. S-2 was to rectify defects in the summary administration provisions of the Bankruptcy Act, and those defects would not be overcome by this particular bill. Second, I feel that the legislation to come forward will probably set out the procedure to be followed by parties in connection with such a consolidation order, and their various rights at that stage, more clearly than the hon. member has. Third, I feel, as I have already pointed out, that his provisions with regard to unconscionable transactions are premature at this time, in view of the fact that their subject matter is now before the Supreme Court of Canada on an appeal.

Mr. Speaker, I rise for a minute or two to express my support for the principle and purpose of this bill. I am sure the hon. member has been moved to introduce it because of his knowledge of injustices suffered by many individuals. I must explain that I am not capable of dealing with the intricacies of the law: I am not a lawyer. I have had to work hard all my life for my living, but I have had an interest in this subject for many years. Quite a number of my constituents, working people and businessmen, have been done out of considerable sums of money by nothing more nor less than damned crooks who have fled to the United States after they have fleeced good Canadians. More than that, to my knowledge the federal and provincial governments have lost thousands of dollars in taxation in my riding on that account, and nothing can be done about it.

Bankruptcy Act
I could give endless illustrations, and they have made me come to the conclusion that we need a complete overhaul of the Bankruptcy Act. I think reference of this bill to the appropriate committee will give the committee an opportunity to call witnesses, hear evidence, study this situation and make a report to the house.
I find that the majority of people are completely ignorant as to their rights under the Bankruptcy Act. I think the act and the procedures require simplifying and in my opinion there should be more information with respect to the law and the regulations available to ordinary persons, in language they can understand. I can think of numerous instances of good, honest people losing considerable sums of money, and on some occasions suffering to quite an extent, because of their ignorance of the present law and their failure even to take advantage of certain provisions of it.
I know this is a complex question, Mr. Speaker. As I have said, I am not capable of going into the finer points of the legislation, but I do feel that if the bill is referred to the appropriate committee this will provide an opportunity for us to begin to break ground in the direction of necessary amendments to the Bankruptcy Act.

Mr. Speaker, the first thing that shocks me to some degree about this bill is, as the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) has stated, its patent and blatant unconstitutionality. It is well known that we on this side of the house are very wary and careful, in any legislation that we support or pass, to guard provincial rights jealously.
(Translation):
We on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, are most sensitive to the feelings of the provinces and especially to the so sensitive feelings of a certain premier of a certain province.
(Text):
For this reason, if for no other, I think we on this side of the house could not possibly support the bill. I would point to one aspect of it which is of interest. That is the fact that in essence, if I judge rightly from the remarks of the hon. member who proposed the bill, it is essentially consumer legislation with which he is concerned. I think he suggested that the bill should go to the committee on consumer credit. The problems that are envisaged by the bill are problems that the insolvent gets into by reason of his capacity or status as a consumer, and I suggest that in this house and throughout the country we
[Mr. Herridge.l
have been very remiss in our consumer legislation in all its aspects, not merely on the credit side.
For instance, we put someone in jail because he plays bingo or operates a bingo game with the proceeds to go to charity; and yet the cola companies can put thousands of dollars under bottle caps, and that is legal. For this reason I suggest that our entire concept, that anything can be said or done under the sacred head of advertising, should be very carefully looked at.
You are absolutely right.

Thank you. I think we should take a look at our consumer legislation as a whole. Our people as consumers need greater protection than they are getting today not only on the credit side but with regard to their whole position as consumers, who are subjected to the continual pressure and heat of advertising and the wrongs and misconceptions of advertising that are foisted upon them as consumers. Therefore I hope that some day in the not too distant future we shall be able to look at this entire picture.

Mr. Speaker, the business for Tuesday and Wednesday was settled very amicably last night, of course, and I shall just reiterate that the government intends to propose that the house go into committee of supply. If there is an amendment it is understood that the vote on the amendment and any subamendment will take place at the end of Tuesday, so that Wednesday will be available for general grievances and the vote on Wednesday will be at a quarter to six. I just reiterate that so it will be available on the record. On Thursday, we propose to continue in committee with the department of industry bill, and to proceed with that bill to its conclusion. Then, we shall take the resolution concerning the Atlantic development board.
I might say that if the department of industry bill should be concluded before five o'clock it would not be possible to begin the resolution concerning the Atlantic bill until eight o'clock, and I would ask my colleague, the President of the Privy Council, to begin

the debate on the second reading of the economic council bill. I would hope we could arrange things so that both of these measures could be considered later that day and the following day. It may be that there will be some further clarification of the business
